title: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email
gist: Attackers hijacked 333 Tor exit nodes between October 2 and 5 to redirect SSH traffic to 12 interception servers and block encrypted email ports to force plaintext, after compromising a Tor management server through a reused password and installing the Ebury backdoor; the culprit and the means of mass access remain unknown.

insights.claim: Unknown attackers compromised 333 Tor exit relays and reconfigured them to redirect SSH traffic to one of 12 attacker-controlled interception servers and to block encrypted email ports while allowing unencrypted ones.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Exit-node trust is a systemic weakness for anonymity networks; plaintext fallback paths are exploitable.
insights.locator: Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes

insights.claim: The initial compromise began in late August when the attacker used a reused valid password to access a Tor management server, installed the Ebury Linux backdoor, then pivoted over SSH to a second server called Switzerland2.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Credential reuse remains the entry point for infrastructure-level compromises.
insights.locator: The hijacking began in late August

insights.claim: The attackers blocked ports 25, 465, 587, 993 and 995, used for encrypted email, while leaving unencrypted ports open, so services that downgraded to plaintext would expose messages; it is unclear if any downgrades succeeded.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Opportunistic TLS fallback is an exposure; enforcing encrypted-only mail closes it.

insights.claim: Users who ignored the SSH host key changed warning would enter passwords on attacker servers, which stole the password, watched typed commands, and then opened a second connection to infect the server with Ebury.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Habitual dismissal of host key warnings converts a network hijack into full server compromise.

insights.claim: The hijacking occurred from October 2 to October 5, and Tor volunteer Kaba detected it by polling about 3,000 exit nodes for correct SSH fingerprints and running a honeypot to watch the interception software.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Active fingerprint monitoring can catch exit-node tampering.
insights.locator: The hijacking occurred from October 2 to October 5.

insights.claim: Investigators do not know how the attackers gained control of so many underlying servers, with a hosting-company breach one inconclusive theory, nor why Switzerland2 accepted an RSA key not in its authorized keys.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Root cause unknown, so similar compromises could recur.

insights.claim: The Tor volunteer speculates that use of Ebury and broad collection of unencrypted data point to a financially motivated crime group, though this is speculation.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.quote: The use of Ebury and the broad collection of unencrypted data point to a financially motivated crime group

insights.claim: Defense in depth is the lesson: configure email accounts to accept only encrypted traffic and reject unencrypted ports, and disable SSH password authentication in favor of keys.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: These two controls would have neutralized both attack branches.
